title: The Burning Bakery of Hanuman Tekri and the Duty of a Trial Judge
hook: After thirty-seven witnesses turned hostile in a massacre trial, the Supreme Court ordered an unprecedented out-of-state retrial and jailed a perjuring witness.
laws: Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Section 302, Section 149, Section 193, and Section 436)
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Section 311 and Section 406)
Constitution of India (Article 21, Article 129, Article 136, and Article 142)

facts.label: Court
facts.value: Supreme Court of India (Criminal Appellate and Contempt Jurisdiction)

facts.label: Incident
facts.value: Arson attack on a two-story bakery in Hanuman Tekri, Vadodara on March 1, 2002, killing fourteen people

facts.label: Initial Trial Outcome
facts.value: Thirty-seven of forty-three prosecution witnesses turned hostile; all twenty-one accused acquitted in June 2003

facts.label: Retrial Outcome
facts.value: Trial transferred to Maharashtra; special court convicted nine accused to life imprisonment in February 2006

summary: On the night of March 1, 2002, an armed mob encircled and torched a two-story bakery in the Hanuman Tekri neighborhood of Vadodara, killing fourteen people trapped inside. A nineteen-year-old survivor named twenty-one attackers in a hospital police statement, but when the fast-track trial opened in May 2003, thirty-seven of forty-three prosecution witnesses retracted their statements and all twenty-one accused were acquitted.

After fleeing to Mumbai, the star witness alleged that death threats from local political figures had forced her courtroom retraction, prompting the National Human Rights Commission and the survivor to move the Supreme Court. On April 12, 2004, the Supreme Court held that the trial was a sham because the prosecutor and trial judge had acted as passive spectators while witnesses were intimidated, and invoked Article 142 and Section 406 to transfer the retrial out of Gujarat to Mumbai.

During the Mumbai retrial, however, the same star witness reversed her story a second time and claimed she had been coerced by activists, leading the Supreme Court to order a forensic financial inquiry by its Registrar General. When unexplained bank deposits exposed deliberate, paid perjury, the court sentenced her to one year of simple imprisonment for contempt on March 8, 2006, while the Mumbai special court relied on steadfast eyewitnesses and forensic evidence to convict nine killers.

judgment.outcome: Acquittals quashed and de novo retrial transferred to Maharashtra (2004); star witness later convicted of criminal contempt and sentenced to one year of simple imprisonment and a fifty-thousand-rupee fine (2006).
points: A criminal trial judge is not a mere tape recorder or mute spectator; under Section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act and Section 311 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the judge has an active duty to question and summon witnesses to discover the truth.
The fundamental right to a fair trial under Article 21 belongs equally to victims, witnesses, and society, requiring the State to protect witnesses from intimidation.
Under Article 142 and Section 406, the Supreme Court may transfer a criminal trial outside a state when local intimidation makes an impartial trial impossible.
The testimony of a hostile witness is not automatically erased; courts may accept corroborated portions, while witnesses who accept inducements to lie under oath face summary punishment for contempt.

principles.name: Active Judicial Truth-Seeking
principles.meaning: A trial judge has an affirmative statutory duty to intervene, question witnesses, and summon essential evidence rather than passively recording coerced retractions.
principles.inThisCase: The Supreme Court held that the fast-track judge abdicated his duty under Section 165 of the Evidence Act and Section 311 of the procedural code when dozens of witnesses suddenly recanted.

principles.name: Triangulation of Fair Trial Rights
principles.meaning: Fairness in criminal justice requires balancing the rights of the accused, the victim, and the broader public interest.
principles.inThisCase: Because witness intimidation destroyed the integrity of the Vadodara trial, the court declared the acquittals a nullity and ordered a fresh trial in another state.

principles.name: Separating Grain from Chaff in Hostile Testimony
principles.meaning: When a witness turns hostile, the court need not discard their entire testimony if parts of it are reliable and corroborated by independent evidence.
principles.inThisCase: During the Mumbai retrial, the special court convicted nine perpetrators using steadfast witnesses alongside forensic and medical records despite the star witness's second reversal.

takeaways: Trial judges must actively use statutory questioning and witness-summoning powers when intimidation threatens to derail justice.
Witness protection is a constitutional necessity under Article 21, not an optional administrative courtesy.
Deliberate perjury and paid reversals by a witness undermine the justice system and attract criminal contempt sanctions.

social.hook: What happens when thirty-seven eyewitnesses to a deadly bakery arson suddenly claim in court they saw nothing?
social.script: What happens when thirty-seven eyewitnesses to a deadly bakery arson suddenly claim in court they saw nothing? In March 2002, fourteen people died in a Vadodara bakery fire. After thirty-seven witnesses turned hostile, all twenty-one accused walked free. When the star witness fled to Mumbai alleging death threats, the Supreme Court quashed the acquittals, ruled that a trial judge cannot sit as a mute spectator, and transferred the retrial to Maharashtra. Then came a twist: she turned hostile again. A forensic financial inquiry uncovered paid perjury, landing her in jail for contempt while nine killers were convicted. You be the judge. Full case notes are on the Courtroom Chronicles website.

carousel.heading: The 2002 Bakery Arson
carousel.text: Fourteen people died when an armed mob torched a Vadodara bakery, yet thirty-seven witnesses turned hostile at trial.

carousel.heading: The Acquittal Shock
carousel.text: All twenty-one accused were acquitted after the prosecutor and trial judge failed to question the sudden retractions.

carousel.heading: The Legal Question
carousel.text: Can an appellate court order an out-of-state retrial when local witness intimidation destroys the fairness of a trial?

carousel.heading: Retrial and Contempt
carousel.text: The Supreme Court transferred the retrial to Mumbai, where nine killers were convicted and the perjuring star witness was jailed.

carousel.heading: Why It Matters
carousel.text: The ruling established that judges must actively seek truth and that witness protection is essential to Article 21.
